opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot you can do from inside a company, and a lot of it is less glamorous than people imagine.

One bucket I'm really excited about is what I'd call making safety commitments concrete and checkable. Things like responsible scaling policies or frontier safety frameworks, where the company says ahead of time: here are the dangerous capabilities we're watching for, here's how we'll test for them, and here are the protective measures we'll have in place before we go past certain thresholds. I like that because it doesn't require everyone to agree on how likely catastrophe is. It's more of an "if-then" structure: *if* we see these warning signs, *then* we do these things. That's something both skeptics and worried people can sign up for, and it creates a template other companies and eventually regulators can build on.

A second bucket is security. I think it's underrated how much of the risk picture depends on whether model weights can be stolen, by state actors or anyone else. If you develop something extremely capable and it walks out the door, a lot of your other careful work stops mattering. So getting to really serious security, the kind that could hold up against well-resourced attackers, seems like one of the highest-leverage things a company can invest in, and it's an area where there's a real talent shortage.

Third, there's alignment and control research, especially the kind that's only really possible with access to frontier models. Studying whether models are scheming or deceiving, building monitoring setups, figuring out how you'd catch a model trying to undermine you, and designing protocols so that even a model that isn't fully trustworthy can be used relatively safely. Being inside a leading company gives you access to the most capable systems, the compute, and the chance to get techniques actually adopted rather than just published.

And then there's a softer but important category: being a person inside the company who helps shape decisions and culture. Making sure that when there's a tradeoff between moving fast and being careful, someone is raising the right considerations, that there are good internal processes, and that the company is setting a positive example on things like transparency and how it engages with policymakers. A company can demonstrate that you can be at the frontier *and* take these risks seriously, and that matters a lot for what the rest of the industry thinks is normal.

I'd add one caveat: I don't think any of this gets us to a world where things are clearly safe. A lot of it is about making the situation meaningfully better than it would otherwise be: cheap, practical measures that reduce risk at the margin. I think that's still very worth doing.

r001.rationale: It says a company’s example can shape what the industry considers normal, but does not explain that making measures commercially practical increases other companies’ likelihood of adopting them.

r002.rationale: It mentions setting a positive example on transparency and policymaker engagement, but does not connect perceived responsibility to benefits that pressure competitors to prioritize safety.

r003.rationale: It does not state that safety competition could prompt rivals to devise risk-reduction measures the original company has not developed.

r004.rationale: It mentions transparency generally, but does not recommend sharing evidence about the company’s own models regardless of competitors’ actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people hear "working at an AI company" and picture one thing, which is you're building the models and maybe you're on some safety team doing alignment research. And that's real, that matters, but I actually think some of the highest-leverage stuff is a bit less glamorous than that.

The thing I keep coming back to is what I'd call the "responsible scaling" cluster of work. The basic idea is: can a company commit, in advance and in writing, to specific things it will do as its models get more capable? Like, "if a model can do X, we will not deploy it until we have safeguards Y and Z in place." And then can you actually build the internal machinery to make those commitments mean something? That's a huge amount of unsexy work. You need people figuring out what the dangerous capabilities even are, you need evaluations that can detect them, you need a security posture that's good enough that the weights don't just walk out the door, and you need governance so that when the evals say something uncomfortable, the answer isn't just "well, we're launching anyway."

I'm excited about that because I think it does a couple of things at once. One, it directly makes the company safer. Two, it creates a template. If one lab does it credibly, it's much easier to say to other labs, "why don't you have this?" and much easier for governments to say, "okay, this is what we're going to require." I think a lot of good policy is going to end up looking like codifying things that at least one responsible actor has already shown is feasible.

The second thing I'd highlight is security, and I'd put it almost on par with alignment. If you can't protect the weights, a lot of your other safety work doesn't matter, because someone else can just take the model and strip out whatever you've done. And frontier labs are nowhere near where they'd need to be to resist, say, a determined state actor. So people who have serious security chops working on that problem seem really valuable to me, and it's a career path that doesn't require you to have an opinion about every philosophical debate in AI safety.

Third, I'd say the evaluation and dangerous capabilities science. We need to actually be able to answer the question "how dangerous is this model" in a way that's rigorous enough that a skeptic would accept it. Right now that's shockingly immature. People at labs have unusually good access to the models and to the compute to run those tests at scale.

And then the last one is more of a cultural and institutional thing. There's a lot of value in just having people inside who are willing to be the person who says "I'm not comfortable with this" in the room, and who have enough credibility and enough of a track record that they get taken seriously. That's hard to measure, and I don't want to oversell it, because there's a real risk of just getting captured by the environment and telling yourself you're the conscience of the place while going along with everything. But I do think when I look at the cases where a lab has done something more cautious than it had to, it's often because specific people pushed for it.

I'd add one caveat to all of this, which is that I think you should go in with your eyes open. Working at a lab means you're accelerating the thing you're worried about to some degree. I think it's often still worth it, but I'd want people to be honest with themselves about that tradeoff, to keep ties to people outside the company who can tell them when they're rationalizing, and to be willing to leave if the place stops being one where safety work can actually win arguments.

r001.rationale: The response says a credible lab can make its approach easier for other labs and governments to adopt or require, but it does not explain that making risk-reduction measures commercially practical increases adoption.

r002.rationale: It describes a template that others can point to, but does not say that reputational benefits from being seen as responsible pressure competitors to compete on safety.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that safety competition could lead rivals to devise risk-reduction measures the original company has not developed.

r004.rationale: The response does not recommend sharing evidence about the company’s models to inform the public regardless of competitors’ actions.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest opportunities is to get a company to be really explicit about what would cause it to slow down or stop. What capabilities would an AI system have to demonstrate before you’d say, “We need stronger safeguards before we go any further”? And what would those safeguards actually have to accomplish?

That gives you a concrete research agenda. You need evaluations that can tell you when you’re approaching dangerous capabilities. You need to know how secure your systems are, and whether your measures for controlling them actually work. And you need a decision-making process that can act on those findings, including when acting is costly for the company.

I’m especially interested in work that connects the technical details to those decisions. It’s one thing to say, “We care about safety.” It’s another to have people who can explain to leadership, “Here’s what we tested, here’s what we still don’t know, and here’s why this next step would be a bad idea.”

There’s also an opportunity for a leading company to make practices like that easier for others to adopt, and easier for governments to require. I wouldn’t want the whole plan to rest on companies voluntarily doing the right thing. But work inside a company can help make stronger external oversight practical.

r001.rationale: The response says practices could be easier for other companies to adopt, but does not explain that making them commercially practical increases adoption.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reputational benefits from being seen as responsible or pressure on competitors to compete on safety.

r003.rationale: It does not state that safety competition could lead rivals to develop measures the original company has not devised.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend sharing evidence about the company’s own models regardless of competitors’ behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
One strategy I’m particularly excited about is getting a company to make clear commitments in advance about what it will do as its AI systems become more capable. You don’t want to wait until you have a very powerful system, with a lot of pressure to deploy it, and then start asking what level of risk is acceptable.

You want to say ahead of time: here are capabilities that would be warning signs; here’s how we’re going to test for them; and here are the safeguards we would need before we could responsibly go further. If we can’t put those safeguards in place, we need to be willing to pause further development or deployment.

That creates a lot of concrete work inside a company. Can you build evaluations that actually tell you whether a model can do something dangerous? Can you secure the model well enough that someone can’t just steal it? Can you make a convincing case that the safeguards work, and make sure the people deciding whether to proceed have access to the evidence?

I also think a leading company can help make those practices standard across the industry and eventually inform regulation. A voluntary commitment by one company has limitations. But a company that develops a workable approach, follows it, and supports holding its competitors to comparable standards could make a pretty substantial difference.

r001.rationale: The response says a workable approach could become an industry standard, but does not explain that making measures commercially practical would increase other companies’ likelihood of adopting them.

r002.rationale: It does not mention benefits from being perceived as responsible or pressure on competitors to compete on safety.

r003.rationale: It says competitors could be held to comparable standards, but does not state that rivals may develop measures the original company has not devised.

r004.rationale: It discusses giving decision-makers evidence about safeguards, but does not recommend sharing evidence about the company’s models publicly regardless of competitors’ behavior.
